notes:
1. Meaning of Anti-Corruption Measures

Anti-Corruption Measures are policies, laws, institutions and administrative practices designed to:

  • Prevent corruption.
  • Detect corruption.
  • Investigate wrongdoing.
  • Punish offenders.
  • Promote transparency.
  • Strengthen accountability.
  • Encourage ethical governance.
  • Their larger objective is to ensure that public power is exercised only in the public interest.

2. Need for Anti-Corruption Measures

Anti-corruption measures are necessary because corruption:

  • Weakens democratic institutions.
  • Reduces economic growth.
  • Wastes public funds.
  • Increases inequality.
  • Delays development.
  • Discourages investment.
  • Violates constitutional values.
  • Undermines public trust.

3. Major Objectives

The major objectives are:

  • Prevention.
  • Detection.
  • Investigation.
  • Punishment.
  • Transparency.
  • Accountability.
  • Protection of public resources.
  • Efficient administration.
  • Public confidence.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Good Governance.

4. Core Principles

An effective anti-corruption system is based on:

  • Integrity.
  • Transparency.
  • Accountability.
  • Equality.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Public participation.
  • Ethical governance.
  • Fair investigation.
  • Independent institutions.

5. Types of Anti-Corruption Measures

Important categories include:

  • Preventive Measures.
  • Detective Measures.
  • Investigative Measures.
  • Punitive Measures.
  • Corrective Measures.
  • Administrative Measures.
  • Legal Measures.
  • Institutional Measures.
  • Financial Accountability Measures.
  • Technological Measures.
  • Citizen Participation Measures.
  • Ethical Measures.

6. Preventive Measures

Preventive measures aim to:

  • Stop corruption before it occurs.

Examples include:

  • Simplification of procedures.
  • Reduction of unnecessary discretion.
  • Transparency.
  • Digital governance.
  • Rotation of officials.
  • Ethical training.
  • Public awareness.
  • Strong internal controls.

7. Detective Measures

Detective measures identify suspected corruption through:

  • Vigilance inspections.
  • Internal audits.
  • Social audits.
  • Financial audits.
  • Complaint systems.
  • Whistle-blower disclosures.
  • Surprise inspections.

8. Investigation

Investigative measures determine:

  • Whether corruption occurred.
  • Who was responsible.
  • What evidence exists.

Investigations may be conducted by:

  • Vigilance agencies.
  • Police.
  • Anti-corruption agencies.
  • Specialised investigating authorities.

9. Principles of Investigation

Anti-corruption investigations should be:

  • Fair.
  • Independent.
  • Impartial.
  • Lawful.
  • Evidence-based.

10. Punitive Measures

Punitive measures may include:

  • Criminal prosecution.
  • Departmental action.
  • Suspension where legally justified.
  • Dismissal.
  • Recovery of loss where authorised.
  • Imprisonment.
  • Fine.

11. Corrective Measures

  • Corrective measures seek to remove the causes that allowed corruption.

Examples include:

  • Administrative reform.
  • Policy revision.
  • Better supervision.
  • Process simplification.
  • Improved internal controls.
  • Training.
  • Digital monitoring.

12. Preventive vs Punitive

Preventive Measures:

  • Act before corruption occurs.
  • Focus on system improvement.
  • Reduce opportunity.

Punitive Measures:

  • Act after misconduct occurs.
  • Impose legal or disciplinary consequences.
  • Promote deterrence.

13. Detection vs Investigation

Detection:

  • Identifies suspected wrongdoing.
  • May begin from audits, complaints or inspections.

Investigation:

  • Establishes facts.
  • Collects evidence.
  • Determines responsibility.

14. Simplification of Procedures

  • Complex procedures can create opportunities for corruption.

Administrative reform therefore seeks to:

  • Reduce unnecessary approvals.
  • Simplify documentation.
  • Minimise delays.
  • Standardise processes.
  • Reduce discretionary decision-making.

15. Time-Bound Service Delivery

Providing services within fixed time limits:

  • Reduces delays.
  • Limits opportunities for bribery.
  • Improves accountability.
  • Improves citizen satisfaction.
  • The attachment notes that many States have enacted laws for time-bound public services.

16. Rotation of Officials

Periodic transfer or rotation in sensitive posts may:

  • Reduce familiarity-based corruption.
  • Prevent concentration of influence.
  • Reduce misuse of authority.
  • Strengthen impartiality.

17. Internal Control Systems

Internal controls seek to ensure:

  • Compliance with rules.
  • Proper financial management.
  • Prevention of fraud.
  • Detection of irregularities.
  • Clear responsibility.

18. Internal Audit

Internal Audit examines:

  • Financial transactions.
  • Administrative procedures.
  • Rule compliance.
  • Operational efficiency.
  • It helps detect irregularities early.

19. Performance Monitoring

Performance monitoring may include:

  • Periodic reviews.
  • Performance indicators.
  • Service-quality assessments.
  • Departmental inspections.

20. Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988

  • The Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 is a major criminal-law framework dealing with corruption.

The attachment also identifies:

  • Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002.
  • Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, where relevant.
  • Other applicable criminal laws.

21. Departmental Proceedings

Apart from criminal prosecution, public servants may face:

  • Departmental inquiry.
  • Disciplinary proceedings.
  • Administrative penalties.

Departmental proceedings deal with:

  • Service misconduct.

22. Departmental Proceedings vs Criminal Prosecution

Departmental Proceedings:

  • Governed by service rules.
  • Concern service misconduct.
  • May result in disciplinary penalties.

Criminal Prosecution:

  • Governed by criminal law.
  • Determines criminal liability.
  • May result in imprisonment or fine.

23. Asset Declaration

Applicable laws or service rules may require public officials to disclose:

  • Assets.
  • Liabilities.
  • Financial interests.
  • This promotes transparency and helps identify unexplained wealth.

24. Conflict of Interest

A conflict of interest arises when:

  • Private interests may influence official duties.

It may involve:

  • Financial interest.
  • Family interest.
  • Business relationship.
  • Personal association.
  • Future employment interest.

25. Managing Conflict of Interest

Important safeguards include:

  • Disclosure.
  • Recusal.
  • Transfer of decision-making authority.
  • Gift restrictions.
  • Outside-employment restrictions.
  • Asset declarations.
  • Cooling-off rules where applicable.

26. Vigilance Administration

Vigilance Administration seeks to:

  • Detect misconduct.
  • Prevent corruption.
  • Conduct inquiries.
  • Recommend disciplinary action.
  • Improve systems.

27. Central Vigilance Commission

The Central Vigilance Commission acts as:

  • Apex vigilance institution for Union Government.

Its broad functions include:

  • Supervising vigilance administration.
  • Advising Government departments.
  • Reviewing vigilance matters.
  • Exercising statutory superintendence over specified corruption investigations.

28. Central Bureau of Investigation

The CBI investigates:

  • Corruption cases.
  • Economic offences.
  • Serious crimes referred under law.
  • Court-directed investigations.
  • The attachment describes it as India's premier Central investigating agency.

29. Comptroller and Auditor General

The CAG audits:

  • Government accounts.
  • Public expenditure.
  • Financial management.

Its audit strengthens:

  • Financial accountability.
  • Transparency.
  • Legislative oversight.

30. Central Information Commission

The Central Information Commission promotes transparency through implementation of:

  • Right to Information Act, 2005.
  • Access to information helps reduce opportunities for corruption.

31. Parliamentary Oversight

Parliament exercises oversight through:

  • Question Hour.
  • Budget discussions.
  • Parliamentary Committees.
  • Public Accounts Committee.
  • Estimates Committee.
  • Committee on Public Undertakings.

32. Social Audit

Social Audit enables citizens to examine:

  • Public expenditure.
  • Welfare schemes.
  • Development works.
  • Service delivery.

It strengthens:

  • Transparency.
  • Community participation.
  • Accountability.

33. Financial Audit

Financial Audit examines:

  • Accuracy of accounts.
  • Utilisation of funds.
  • Compliance with financial rules.
  • Financial irregularities.

34. Meaning of Financial Accountability

Financial accountability means ensuring that public money is:

  • Collected lawfully.
  • Managed properly.
  • Spent according to Constitution.
  • Spent according to law.
  • Subject to audit and legislative control.

35. Objectives of Financial Accountability

It aims to:

  • Prevent misuse of funds.
  • Ensure lawful expenditure.
  • Improve financial discipline.
  • Promote efficiency.
  • Protect public resources.
  • Strengthen transparency.

36. Budgetary Control

The Legislature exercises financial control through:

  • Budget approval.
  • Demands for Grants.
  • Appropriation Bills.
  • Finance Bills.
  • Financial discussions.

37. Audit

Audit examines:

  • Accuracy.
  • Legality.
  • Efficiency.
  • Rule compliance.

It can reveal:

  • Waste.
  • Misappropriation.
  • Fraud.
  • Financial irregularity.

38. Public Accounts Committee

The PAC examines:

  • CAG reports.
  • Government expenditure.
  • Financial irregularities.

It recommends:

  • Corrective improvements.

39. Estimates Committee

The Estimates Committee examines:

  • Government expenditure.
  • Economy.
  • Administrative efficiency.

It suggests improvements in:

  • Financial management.

40. Committee on Public Undertakings

The Committee on Public Undertakings examines:

  • Public Sector Undertakings.
  • Efficiency.
  • Financial performance.
  • Accountability.

41. Meaning

Citizen participation means:

  • Active public involvement in governance and administration.

Citizens can strengthen:

  • Transparency.
  • Public monitoring.
  • Accountability.
  • Service delivery.

42. Public Grievance Redress

Citizens should be able to complain about:

  • Delay.
  • Corruption.
  • Misconduct.
  • Deficiency in service.
  • Abuse of authority.

43. Effective Grievance System

A good grievance mechanism should provide:

  • Easy complaint registration.
  • Tracking.
  • Time-bound disposal.
  • Appeal.
  • Responsibility for delay.
  • Feedback to citizens.

44. Public Consultation

Government departments may consult:

  • Citizens.
  • Experts.
  • Stakeholders.
  • Civil society organisations
  • before major public-policy decisions.

45. Meaning of E-Governance

E-Governance is the use of:

  • Information and Communication Technology

for:

  • Government administration.
  • Public service delivery.

46. Objectives of E-Governance

E-Governance seeks to:

  • Improve efficiency.
  • Reduce delay.
  • Increase transparency.
  • Minimise human discretion.
  • Improve accessibility.
  • Strengthen accountability.

47. Important E-Governance Measures

Examples include:

  • Online applications.
  • Digital certificates.
  • Online tax filing.
  • Direct Benefit Transfer.
  • Government e-Marketplace.
  • E-Procurement.
  • Digital land records.
  • E-Office.
  • Online grievance portals.

48. Anti-Corruption Role of E-Governance

E-Governance may reduce corruption by:

  • Reducing physical interaction.
  • Creating digital records.
  • Reducing discretionary decision-making.
  • Tracking applications.
  • Improving traceability.
  • Making payments auditable.

49. Digital Payments

Digital payments promote:

  • Traceability.
  • Audit trails.
  • Reduced cash dependence.
  • Financial transparency.

50. Limits of Technology

  • Technology alone cannot eliminate corruption.

Risks include:

  • Cybercrime.
  • Identity theft.
  • Data breaches.
  • Manipulation of electronic records.
  • Online fraud.
  • Digital exclusion.

51. Ethics in Public Administration

Ethics means:

  • Moral principles guiding public officials.

Ethical administration requires:

  • Honesty.
  • Integrity.
  • Impartiality.
  • Objectivity.
  • Accountability.
  • Public-service orientation.

52. Core Ethical Values

Important values include:

  • Integrity.
  • Honesty.
  • Accountability.
  • Transparency.
  • Objectivity.
  • Impartiality.
  • Compassion.
  • Responsibility.
  • Commitment to public service.

53. Integrity

Integrity means consistency between:

  • Values.
  • Words.
  • Actions.

An officer with integrity:

  • Rejects corruption.
  • Acts honestly.
  • Serves public interest.

54. Transparency

Transparency requires decisions to be:

  • Open.
  • Fair.
  • Documented.
  • Accessible.
  • Subject to public scrutiny.

55. Accountability

Accountability means officials must:

  • Explain decisions.
  • Accept responsibility.
  • Correct mistakes.
  • Comply with law.
  • Answer for misuse of authority.

56. Good Governance

Good Governance means administration that is:

  • Transparent.
  • Accountable.
  • Efficient.
  • Equitable.
  • Responsive.
  • Participatory.
  • Lawful.

57. Principles of Good Governance

Important principles include:

  • Rule of Law.
  • Accountability.
  • Transparency.
  • Participation.
  • Responsiveness.
  • Efficiency.
  • Equity.
  • Inclusiveness.
  • Consensus.
  • Effectiveness.

58. Ethics vs Integrity

Ethics:

  • Moral principles guiding behaviour.

Integrity:

  • Honest application of those principles in actual conduct.

59. Transparency vs Accountability

Transparency:

  • Openness of Government action.

Accountability:

  • Responsibility for Government action.

60. E-Governance vs Good Governance

E-Governance:

  • Technology-based administrative tool.

Good Governance:

  • Overall objective of transparent, accountable and effective administration.

61. Delay in Investigation

Investigations may be delayed due to:

  • Complex transactions.
  • Large evidence volume.
  • Multiple agencies.
  • Cross-border transactions.
  • Procedural requirements.

62. Delay in Trial

Trials may take time because of:

  • Heavy judicial workload.
  • Complex legal issues.
  • Large numbers of witnesses.
  • Procedural delay.

63. Political Interference

Improper political influence may affect:

  • Investigations.
  • Transfers.
  • Administrative decisions.
  • Enforcement action.

64. Weak Enforcement

Even strong laws fail where:

  • Investigations are poor.
  • Prosecution is weak.
  • Departmental action is delayed.
  • Conviction is uncertain.

65. Administrative Complexity

Excessive:

  • Approvals.
  • Documentation.
  • Delays.
  • Discretion
  • may create corruption opportunities.

66. Lack of Transparency

Corruption becomes easier when administration lacks:

  • Public disclosure.
  • Open decision-making.
  • Access to information.
  • Financial transparency.

67. Weak Accountability

Weak supervision can lead to:

  • Misuse of authority.
  • Delayed disciplinary action.
  • Lack of responsibility.
  • Poor institutional performance.

68. Fear of Reporting

Individuals may hesitate to report corruption because of:

  • Harassment.
  • Victimisation.
  • Transfers.
  • Career consequences.
  • Personal-security concerns.

69. Cross-Border Corruption

Modern corruption may involve:

  • Offshore accounts.
  • Shell companies.
  • International transfers.
  • Foreign bribery.
  • Concealment of assets abroad.

70. Money Laundering

Illegal corruption proceeds may be concealed using:

  • Layered transactions.
  • Foreign transfers.
  • Front companies.
  • Complex ownership structures.

71. Procurement Risks

Public procurement may be vulnerable to:

  • Bid rigging.
  • Collusion.
  • Favouritism.
  • Inflated pricing.
  • Manipulated tender conditions.

72. Weak Institutional Coordination

Anti-corruption efforts suffer when:

  • Agencies work in isolation.
  • Information sharing is weak.
  • Responsibilities overlap.
  • Coordination is inadequate.

73. Capacity Constraints

Institutions may face:

  • Staff shortages.
  • Limited technical expertise.
  • Inadequate training.
  • Resource shortages.

74. Measures to Overcome Challenges

The attachment recommends:

  • Speedy investigation.
  • Time-bound trials.
  • Independent institutions.
  • Strong vigilance systems.
  • Digital governance.
  • Transparent procurement.
  • Better whistle-blower protection.
  • Ethics training.
  • Public awareness.
  • International cooperation.
  • Capacity building.
  • Strong internal controls.

75. Article 14

Article 14 guarantees:

  • Equality Before Law.
  • Equal Protection of Laws.

Its anti-corruption relevance is:

  • No arbitrary State action.
  • No unequal protection from lawful accountability.

76. Article 16

Article 16 guarantees:

  • Equality of opportunity in public employment.

It promotes:

  • Merit.
  • Fair selection.
  • Non-discrimination.
  • Reduced nepotism and favouritism.

77. Article 19(1)(a)

Article 19(1)(a) protects:

  • Freedom of Speech and Expression.

It supports:

  • Investigative journalism.
  • Exposure of corruption.
  • Public criticism.
  • Citizen participation.
  • Access to information as judicially developed.

78. Article 32

Article 32 empowers:

  • Supreme Court
  • to enforce Fundamental Rights through writs.

79. Article 39A

Article 39A provides:

  • Equal Justice.
  • Free Legal Aid.

80. Article 50

Article 50 directs:

  • Separation of Judiciary from Executive.
  • This strengthens impartial adjudication and judicial independence.

81. Article 51A

Article 51A contains Fundamental Duties such as:

  • Upholding Constitution.
  • Preserving national integrity.
  • Safeguarding public property.
  • Striving towards excellence.

82. Article 75(3)

Article 75(3) provides:

  • Union Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.
  • Article 75(3) → Union Council of Ministers → Collective Responsibility to Lok Sabha

83. Article 164(2)

Article 164(2) provides:

  • State Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly.
  • Article 164(2) → State Council of Ministers → Legislative Assembly

84. Article 148

Article 148 establishes:

  • Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
  • Article 148 → CAG

85. Articles 149–151

These Articles deal with:

  • CAG duties and powers.
  • Form of accounts.
  • Audit reports.
  • Submission of reports to Legislatures.

86. Article 265

Article 265 provides:

  • No tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.

87. Article 266

Article 266 deals with:

  • Consolidated Fund of India.
  • Consolidated Fund of each State.
  • Public Accounts.

88. Article 267

Article 267 provides for:

  • Contingency Fund of India.
  • Contingency Funds of States.

89. Article 280

Article 280 provides for:

  • Finance Commission.

90. Article 311

Article 311 provides procedural safeguards relating to:

  • Dismissal.
  • Removal.
  • Reduction in rank
  • of specified civil servants.
  • These safeguards do not prevent lawful disciplinary action.

91. Article 312

Article 312 permits creation of:

  • All India Services
  • in the national interest.

92. Article 323A

Article 323A provides for:

  • Administrative Tribunals
  • for service matters.

93. Article 323B

Article 323B permits tribunals for specified areas including:

  • Taxation.
  • Labour.
  • Land reforms.
  • Other constitutionally listed subjects.

94. Article 361

Article 361 grants limited constitutional immunities to:

  • President.
  • Governors
  • during tenure.
  • These do not remove constitutional accountability of public administration.

95. Tenth Schedule

The Tenth Schedule contains:

  • Anti-Defection Law.

It seeks to reduce:

  • Political opportunism.
  • Office-based inducement.
  • Unethical switching of allegiance.

96. Forty-Second Amendment, 1976

The 42nd Amendment:

  • Added Integrity to Preamble.
  • Inserted Fundamental Duties.
  • Expanded Directive Principles.
  • Introduced Administrative Tribunal provisions.

97. Forty-Fourth Amendment, 1978

The 44th Amendment strengthened:

  • Rule of Law.
  • Civil liberties.
  • Constitutional accountability.
  • Protection against arbitrary action.

98. Fifty-Second Amendment, 1985

The 52nd Amendment:

  • Inserted Tenth Schedule.
  • Introduced Anti-Defection Law.

99. Sixty-First Amendment, 1988

The 61st Amendment reduced voting age:

  • 21 years → 18 years.

It expanded:

  • Democratic participation.
  • Electoral accountability.

100. Seventy-Third Amendment, 1992

The 73rd Amendment strengthened:

  • Panchayats.
  • Gram Sabha.
  • State Election Commission.
  • State Finance Commission.
  • Grassroots accountability.

101. Seventy-Fourth Amendment, 1992

The 74th Amendment strengthened:

  • Municipalities.
  • Urban participation.
  • Local accountability.
  • Financial oversight.

102. Ninety-First Amendment, 2003

The 91st Amendment:

  • Strengthened Anti-Defection Law.
  • Removed split protection.
  • Limited size of Council of Ministers.
  • Restricted certain defectors from ministerial office.
  • 91st Amendment → Stronger Anti-Defection + Ministry Size Limit

103. Ninety-Seventh Amendment, 2011

The 97th Amendment promoted:

  • Cooperative-society accountability.
  • Democratic management.
  • Transparency.
  • Its operation was later affected by judicial interpretation.

104. One Hundred and First Amendment, 2016

The 101st Amendment introduced:

  • GST.
  • Article 246A.
  • Article 269A.
  • Article 279A.
  • GST Council.

105. GST and Anti-Corruption

The attachment links GST with:

  • Electronic compliance.
  • Digital audit trails.
  • Better invoice matching.
  • Greater transparency.
  • Reduced scope for certain tax-evasion practices.

106. 102nd and 105th Amendments

The attachment notes:

  • 102nd Amendment, 2018 → Constitutional status to NCBC.
  • 105th Amendment, 2021 → Restored States' authority over SEBC lists for State purposes.
  • Their anti-corruption relevance is described as indirect.

107. State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain, 1975

The Supreme Court recognised:

  • Citizens' Right to Know about Government functioning
  • subject to lawful limitations.
  • Raj Narain → 1975 → Right to Know

108. K. Veeraswami v. Union of India, 1991

  • The Supreme Court held that higher judicial officers are not beyond anti-corruption law.

At the same time, safeguards were prescribed to protect:

  • Judicial independence.

The attachment states that prior permission of:

  • Chief Justice of India
  • was required before investigation against a sitting higher-court Judge under the framework laid down by Court.

109. Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997

The case concerned:

  • Political interference.
  • Delay in corruption investigations involving senior public officials.

110. Vineet Narain Principle

The Supreme Court strengthened:

  • CVC supervision.
  • CBI accountability.
  • Independent investigation.
  • Institutional continuity.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Vineet Narain → 1997 → Independent Corruption Investigation

111. Association for Democratic Reforms, 2002

The Supreme Court directed candidates to disclose:

  • Criminal antecedents.
  • Assets.
  • Liabilities.
  • Educational qualifications.
  • ADR → 2002 → Candidate Disclosure

112. PUCL v. Union of India, 2003

The Court reaffirmed:

  • Voters' Right to Know.
  • Electoral transparency.
  • Candidate-disclosure principles.

113. P.J. Thomas Case, 2011

Centre for PIL v. Union of India concerned appointment of:

  • Central Vigilance Commissioner.

114. Institutional Integrity Principle

  • The Supreme Court invalidated the appointment because relevant integrity concerns had not been properly considered.

The Court emphasised:

  • Institutional Integrity.
  • P.J. Thomas Case → 2011 → Institutional Integrity

115. Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh, 2012

The case concerned delay in deciding:

  • Prosecution sanction.

The Supreme Court held such requests must be considered:

  • Within a reasonable period.
  • Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh → 2012 → Timely Prosecution Sanction

116. 2G Spectrum Case, 2012

Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India concerned:

  • 2G Spectrum licences.

The Supreme Court:

  • Found allocation arbitrary and unconstitutional.
  • Cancelled 122 licences.
  • Emphasised transparent public-resource allocation.
  • 2G Case → 2012 → 122 Licences Cancelled

117. Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh, 2013

The Supreme Court held:

  • FIR registration is generally mandatory where information discloses a cognizable offence.
  • Preliminary inquiry is permitted only in limited categories identified by Court.

118. Lily Thomas v. Union of India, 2013

  • The Supreme Court invalidated statutory protection that allowed convicted sitting legislators to avoid immediate disqualification.

The judgment strengthened:

  • Political accountability.
  • Legislative integrity.
  • Equality before law.
  • Lily Thomas → 2013 → Convicted Legislators + Disqualification

119. Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI, 2014

The Supreme Court struck down:

  • Section 6A of DSPE Act.

It held that senior official rank cannot justify:

  • Unequal protection from corruption investigation.
  • Subramanian Swamy v. Director CBI → 2014 → Section 6A Unconstitutional

120. Coal Block Allocation Case, 2014

Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary concerned:

  • Coal Block allocations.

The Supreme Court held the allocation process:

  • Arbitrary.
  • Legally unsustainable.
  • Numerous allocations were subsequently cancelled.

121. Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India, 2018

The Supreme Court addressed:

  • Criminalisation of politics.

It directed greater disclosure and publicity of:

  • Pending criminal cases of candidates.
  • It also encouraged stronger legislative reform.

122. Common Judicial Principles

The attachment identifies the following principles:

  • No public official is above law.
  • Corruption investigations must be protected from improper interference.
  • Prosecution sanction should not be indefinitely delayed.
  • Rank cannot provide unequal protection from investigation.
  • Public resources must be allocated transparently.
  • Voters have a Right to Know.
  • Institutional integrity matters in vigilance appointments.
  • Public office is a public trust.

What are Anti-Corruption Measures? → Laws, policies, institutions and administrative practices used to prevent, detect, investigate and punish corruption.

What is their main objective? → Ensure public power is exercised only for public interest.

What are the four basic stages? → Prevention, Detection, Investigation and Punishment.

What are Preventive Measures? → Measures that reduce opportunities for corruption before it occurs.

Give examples. → Procedure simplification, transparency, rotation, digital governance and ethical training.

What are Detective Measures? → Audits, complaints, vigilance inspections, social audits and whistle-blower disclosures.

What is the difference between Detection and Investigation? → Detection identifies suspected corruption; investigation collects evidence and establishes responsibility.

What are Corrective Measures? → Reforms intended to prevent recurrence of similar corruption.

Why is simplification of procedures important? → It reduces delay and discretion.

Why are officials rotated in sensitive posts? → To reduce familiarity-based corruption and concentration of influence.

What is Internal Audit? → Examination of transactions, procedures and compliance within an organisation.

What is the difference between Departmental Proceedings and Criminal Prosecution? → Departmental proceedings address service misconduct; criminal prosecution determines criminal guilt.

Why are asset declarations useful? → They increase transparency and may help identify unexplained wealth.

What is Conflict of Interest? → Situation where private interests may improperly influence official duties.

How can it be controlled? → Disclosure, recusal, gift restrictions, asset declarations and other safeguards.

What is Vigilance Administration? → Administrative system for preventing, detecting and responding to misconduct and corruption.

What is the role of CVC in the attachment? → Apex vigilance institution for Union Government.

What is the role of CBI? → Investigation of corruption, economic offences and specified serious crimes.

What is the role of CAG? → Audit of Government finances and public expenditure.

What is the role of CIC? → Promote transparency under RTI framework.

Which Parliamentary Committee examines CAG reports? → Public Accounts Committee.

What does Estimates Committee examine? → Government expenditure, economy and administrative efficiency.

What does Committee on Public Undertakings examine? → Public Sector Undertakings.

What is Financial Accountability? → Lawful collection, management and expenditure of public money.

How does Legislature exercise financial control? → Budget, Demands for Grants, Appropriation Bills and Finance Bills.

What is Social Audit? → Citizen examination of Government expenditure, schemes and public works.

What is Public Grievance Redress? → Mechanism to complain against delay, corruption, misconduct or poor service.

What is E-Governance? → Use of ICT in Government administration and service delivery.

Name major E-Governance tools in the attachment. → DBT, GeM, E-Procurement, digital land records, e-Office and online grievance portals.

How does E-Governance reduce corruption? → By reducing physical interaction, discretion and cash use while creating digital records and audit trails.

Can technology alone eliminate corruption? → No.

What risks remain? → Cybercrime, data breaches, manipulation of records and digital exclusion.

What is Ethics in Public Administration? → Moral principles guiding public officials.

What is Integrity? → Consistent honest application of values in conduct.

What is Transparency? → Openness of Government action.

What is Accountability? → Responsibility and answerability for official decisions.

What is Good Governance? → Transparent, accountable, efficient, equitable, responsive and lawful administration.

Which Article guarantees Equality Before Law? → Article 14.

Which Article promotes merit in public employment? → Article 16.

Which Article supports investigative journalism and exposure of corruption? → Article 19(1)(a).

Which Article provides Constitutional Remedies? → Article 32.

Which Article provides Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid? → Article 39A.

Which Article directs separation of Judiciary from Executive? → Article 50.

Which Article contains Fundamental Duties? → Article 51A.

Which Article makes Union Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Lok Sabha? → Article 75(3).

Which Article establishes CAG? → Article 148.

Which Articles deal with CAG powers and reports? → Articles 149–151.

Which Article makes State Council of Ministers collectively responsible to Assembly? → Article 164(2).

Which Article provides taxation only by authority of law? → Article 265.

Which Article deals with Consolidated Funds? → Article 266.

Which Article deals with Contingency Funds? → Article 267.

Which Article provides Finance Commission? → Article 280.

Which Article protects civil servants through procedural safeguards? → Article 311.

Which Article deals with All India Services? → Article 312.

Which Article deals with Administrative Tribunals? → Article 323A.

Which Article deals with other specified Tribunals? → Article 323B.

Which Schedule contains Anti-Defection Law? → Tenth Schedule.

Which Amendment inserted it? → 52nd Amendment, 1985.

Which Amendment strengthened it? → 91st Amendment, 2003.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Panchayats? → 73rd Amendment.

Which Amendment constitutionalised Municipalities? → 74th Amendment.

Which Amendment introduced GST? → 101st Amendment, 2016.

Which case recognised citizens' Right to Know? → State of Uttar Pradesh v. Raj Narain, 1975.

Which case is the leading anti-corruption institutional judgment? → Vineet Narain v. Union of India, 1997.

What did Vineet Narain strengthen? → Independent investigation, CVC supervision and CBI accountability.

Which case introduced the principle of Institutional Integrity in vigilance appointments? → P.J. Thomas Case, 2011.

Which case dealt with delay in prosecution sanction? → Subramanian Swamy v. Manmohan Singh, 2012.

Which case cancelled 122 telecom licences? → 2G Spectrum Case, 2012.

Which case held FIR registration generally mandatory for cognizable offences? → Lalita Kumari, 2013.

Which case strengthened disqualification of convicted legislators? → Lily Thomas, 2013.

Which case struck down Section 6A of DSPE Act? → Subramanian Swamy v. Director, CBI, 2014.

Which case dealt with arbitrary Coal Block allocations? → Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary, 2014.

Which case dealt with criminalisation of politics? → Public Interest Foundation v. Union of India, 2018.

What is the easiest summary of the chapter? → Effective anti-corruption governance requires prevention, transparency, independent investigation, financial accountability, ethical administration, citizen participation and lawful punishment.
